t.8.1: Right after the rite of the clasping of hands, the body of the daughter of the king of mountains, taking on both love and shyness toward Hara, became enchanting, the very object of Kāma's longing.
t.8.2: When spoken to, she gave no reply; when her garment was caught hold of, she wished to go; she lay upon the couch with her face turned away; yet even so she was a source of delight to Pinākin.
t.8.3: When her beloved lay feigning sleep, Pārvatī, out of curiosity, let her gaze fall upon his face; and as he opened his eyes with a smile, she shut hers as though struck by lightning.
t.8.5: "Friend, in private you should attend upon Śaṅkara in this way, with your timidity held in check": so her companions had instructed her, but she, flustered, did not remember it when her beloved stood before her.
t.8.4: Śaṅkara's hand, placed upon the region of her navel, was held back by her as she trembled; and then her silken garment, of its own accord, came to have its waist-knot loosened far apart.
t.8.6: When the chastiser of Anaṅga, eager to start a conversation, plied her with questions even about trifling matters, Pārvatī received them with a glance and gave her answer only by a movement of her head.
t.8.7: In private, her garment stripped away, she covered both eyes of Śūlin with her two palms; but since the eye in his forehead still saw, she was left distressed by her futile effort.
t.8.9: The taking of her face in a kiss that left her lower lip unbruised, the nail-mark that was given without leaving a wound, and the lovemaking of her beloved that was gentle: that Pārvatī endured, and nothing else.
t.8.8: Though she withheld her lip in kisses, though her hands went limp in his unsparing embrace, though her passion was constrained and any response was hard to win, the bride's lovemaking was still dear to the Lord.
t.8.10: At daybreak, out of shyness, she did not satisfy the curiosity of her friends, who were eager to question her about what had happened in the night, yet in her heart she longed to tell them.
t.8.12: Seeing her, whose youth had been enjoyed by Nīlakaṇṭha, her mother was comforted; for a bride, by being dear to her husband, casts away the sorrow in her mother's heart.
t.8.11: And as she looked in the mirror at the marks of their lovemaking, seeing the reflection of her beloved, seated behind her, appear beside her own reflection, what things did she not do out of bashfulness!
t.8.13: For some days, lovemaking was somehow carried on by Sthāṇu and by her; then, having come to know the delight of love, little by little she gave up her habit of finding lovemaking painful.
t.8.14: Pressed against his chest, she embraced her beloved; she did not turn away the face he sought, and only feebly did she restrain his hand, grown eager to loosen her girdle.
t.8.15: Then, within just a few days, the love between those two grew firm and mutually dependent: revealed through feeling, knowing no unkindness, rich in tender words, and anxious at even a moment's separation.
t.8.16: Just as the bride was devoted to him, a groom worthy of herself, so too was the groom devoted to her; for the Jāhnavī never strays from the ocean, and the ocean, too, finds its one delight in the sweetness of her mouth.
t.8.17: Having in private become the pupil of Śaṃkara, her instructor in the arts of love, whatever skill of a young woman she was taught, that very thing she rendered back to him as her teacher's fee.
t.8.18: Ambikā, her sprout-like hands trembling with the pain, soothed for a moment her lower lip, bitten and then released, with the cool sliver of moon on the crest of the Trident-bearer.
t.8.20: Thus, having favored Manmatha by following the path of the senses' delight, the bull-bannered god Śiva dwelt with Umā in the palace of the king of mountains for a single month.
t.8.19: Śaṅkara, too, offered his forehead-born eye, sullied by powder from her curls during a kiss, to the breath of Pārvatī's mouth, fragrant as a blossoming lotus.
t.8.21: Having taken leave of Himavant, who was wearied by the sorrow of separation from his daughter, the Self-born one wandered here and there, flying about on his humped bull of immeasurable speed.
t.8.22: Reaching Meru on his bull, swift as the wind, the fortunate god enjoyed couches strewn with broken golden sprouts, first pressed by Pārvatī's breasts and able to bear the crushing of love's play.
t.8.23: On the slopes of Mandara, whose rocks bore the marks of Padmanābha's feet and had received fresh drops of nectar, he dwelt, the bee to the lotus of Pārvatī's face.
t.8.24: On the mountain of Ekapiṅgala, the Guru of the world, his neck held in the tight clasp of her arms as she clung to him in fright at the trumpeting of the elephants, enjoyed the clear rays of the moon.
t.8.26: Having struck her beloved with a golden lotus, her eyes closed tight by the water splashed from his hands, Umā plunged into the river in the sky, her girdle echoed by a row of fish.
t.8.25: Once, after his lovemaking on the slopes of Mount Malaya, the southern breeze, shaking the sandalwood creepers and laden with clove blossoms, drank away his beloved's weariness like a flatterer.
t.8.28: Having thus enjoyed, with his beloved as companion, pleasures both heavenly and earthly, Śaṅkara once, when the sunshine was turning red, entered the Gandhamādana mountain.
t.8.27: In the Nandana garden the odd-eyed god long adorned her with pārijāta blossoms worthy of the locks of Puloman's daughter, and the wives of the gods watched him with longing.
t.8.29: There, seated upon a slab of golden rock, he gazed at the sun, now mild enough for the eye to behold, and spoke to his companion in dharma, who was leaning against his left arm.
t.8.30: Having transferred, as it were, the beauty of the lotus into your eyes, whose three parts are tinged with red, yonder lord of the day now withdraws the day, just as the Lord of creatures withdraws the world at the time of universal dissolution.
t.8.31: As the sun sinks low and its rays no longer reach the scattered spray, these waterfalls of your father lose their circling halos of rainbow.
t.8.32: For the pair of cakravākas on the lake, helpless, with strands of lotus filaments held in their beaks, crying out with their necks turned back toward each other, the small distance between them has grown into no small one.
t.8.33: Leaving their daytime haunt, fragrant from the sallakī boughs they have broken, the elephants take up water whose bees lie imprisoned in the closing lotuses, to last them through their roaming until daybreak.
t.8.34: Look, O you of measured speech, at the lake: the sun, hanging at the edge of the western sky, has fashioned with its long reflection what seems a golden causeway across its waters.
t.8.35: Having churned up the pond thick with mud, the tusked leaders of the wild boar herds, who have passed the heat of the day there, now climb out, looking as though they had bitten off brittle lotus-shoots.
t.8.36: This circle of the peacock's tail, perched on the treetop and bright as molten gold, seems to drink in the waning day, the full, broad sunlight of its close.
t.8.37: The sky, its water of sunlight drawn off by Vivasvat, seems on one side to have its mud laid bare by the darkness spreading over the eastern quarter, and it shines like a lake with only a little water left.
t.8.38: With deer entering the courtyards of the leaf-huts and with little trees fresh from the watering of their roots, the hermitages, where the cows for the fire-offering are coming in and the sacred fires have been kindled, wear a lovely splendor.
t.8.39: Though its petals have closed into a bud, the lotus stays for a moment with a small gap still left open, as if lovingly to give room to the bee, who will take up lodging within for the night.
t.8.40: The western quarter, Varuṇa's region, shines with the red sun, whose rays stretch far and can be counted at their tips, like a maiden adorned with a forehead mark of bandhujīva blossom still bearing its filaments.
t.8.41: His companions in their thousands, who drink the heat of his rays, praise the Sun, whose splendour is now passed into the fire, with Sāman hymns whose tones delight the hearts of his chariot-horses.
t.8.42: There he goes to his setting, having laid the day to rest in the great ocean, with his horses whose necks are bowed low, whose eyes are brushed by the chowries at their ears, and whose manes are crushed beneath the yoke.
t.8.43: Now that the sun has set, the sky seems as if asleep; such is the way of a great radiance: as high as it has risen, so far it illumines this world, and when it has fallen from that height, it surely brings the closing of just so much.
t.8.44: Even Saṃdhyā, the Twilight, has followed the venerable form of the Sun as it is laid down upon the peak of the western mountain; how could she not follow in his misfortune him by whom she was once placed in front at his rising?
t.8.45: O curly-haired one, these edges of the clouds glow red, yellow and tawny, as though this Twilight, thinking 'you will see them,' had finely adorned them with her painting brushes.
t.8.46: Look: the evening sunlight seems to have been shared out by the sun among the shaggy manes of the lions, the trees putting forth tender shoots, and the mineral-rich peaks of the mountains.
t.8.48: Therefore you should permit me, too, for a moment, to attend to the observance now at hand; O sweet-voiced one, your friends, skilled in diversion, will keep you entertained.
t.8.47: O daughter of the king of mountains, these ascetics, versed in the sacred rules, having offered handfuls of purifying water, reverently recite the hidden Brahman at the twilight hour for the sake of purification.
t.8.49: Then, curling her lip and intent on ignoring her husband's words, the daughter of the king of mountains began chatting idly, for no reason at all, with Vijayā, who stood close by.
t.8.50: Īśvara, too, having performed with mantras the rite fitting for the close of day, returned to Pārvatī, who had fallen silent out of jealous resentment, and spoke to her again with a smile.
t.8.51: Let go of your anger, you who are angry without cause: it was Saṃdhyā, the Twilight, who made me bow, and no other woman. Do you not know that your own partner in dharma is, like the cakravāka, faithful to his mate alone?
t.8.52: O fair-bodied one, the body that Svayambhū cast off long ago, when the Pitṛs had been created, is this very one that attends both the setting and the rising. Therefore, proud lady, I hold it in reverence.
t.8.53: O daughter of the king of mountains, behold this twilight, now pressed by the growing darkness and lingering on one side only, like a river of liquid red mineral garlanded along one bank with tamāla trees.
t.8.54: The western quarter holds the evening sunlight, all that remains of the sun now set, a streak of red, like the ground of a battlefield holding a blood-stained sword flung down aslant.
t.8.56: The eye's movement reaches neither upward nor downward, neither around nor ahead nor behind; wrapped in floods of darkness, this world at night is like a dwelling in the womb.
t.8.55: Now that the glow born at the meeting of night and day is hidden by Sumeru, this blinding darkness spreads unchecked across all the directions, O long-eyed one.
t.8.57: Whatever is pure or turbid, still or moving, crooked or endowed with the virtue of straightness, all of it alike has been made equal by darkness; fie upon the greatness of the wicked, which takes away all distinction!
t.8.58: Surely, O lotus-faced one, the lord of the sacrificers is rising to drive away the darkness of night, for the face of the eastern quarter is veiled as if with the pollen of ketaka flowers.
t.8.59: The starry night is gazed upon by the hare-bearing moon, its form hidden behind Mandara, just as you, gathered with your dear friends, are watched by me as I stand behind you, listening to your words.
t.8.60: This quarter, whose going forth was held back until the close of day and whose smile of faint moonlight was glimpsed beforehand, now, urged on by Night, pours forth the moon's orb like a secret of the directions.
t.8.61: Look: the moon, glowing with the hue of ripe phalinī fruit, its orb marking both the sky and the water of the lake, mimics a pair of cakravāka birds held far apart by a wide gap.
t.8.62: The freshly risen rays of the lord of plants, soft as the tips of young barley shoots, could be plucked with the pincers of your fingernail-tips to fashion an ornament for your ears.
t.8.63: Gathering up the darkness with his rays, as if seizing a mass of hair with his fingers, the moon seems to kiss the face of Night, whose lotus eyes have closed into buds.
t.8.64: Look, Pārvatī: the sky, its darkness half split by the rays of the young moon, appears like Lake Mānasa, muddied by the bodies of elephants, slowly growing clear again.
t.8.66: The moon's radiance rests upon the lofty places, while the darkness of night is intent on taking refuge in the low. Surely here the Creator has ordained for virtue and vice a course befitting each one's own nature.
t.8.65: Having cast off its redness, this moon has become one whose disc is wholly pure; indeed, a change born of the fault of time does not long endure in those whose nature is spotless.
t.8.67: With drops of water from the moonstones, set flowing by the touch of the moon's rays, the mountain wakes out of season those peacocks sleeping in the trees along its slopes.
t.8.68: Look, lovely one: now the moon, its curiosity stirred, seems to have come to count the strands of the necklaces on the crests of the wish-granting trees with its rays, which appear to flicker there.
t.8.69: Because the mountain rises in heights and sinks into hollows, this moonlight, mingled with darkness, shines like the ornamental paint of a rutting elephant, laid on in patterns of many kinds.
t.8.70: This night-lotus, having drunk in the moon's liquid radiance as it opened, as though unable to hold it, swiftly bursts apart right down to its stalk, letting loose its humming bees.
t.8.71: Look, O fierce one: the garment hanging from the wish-granting tree, its form made uncertain by the pure moonlight, is revealed only when the breeze stirs and it flutters and turns about.
t.8.72: With these flecks of moonlight, broken into fragments by the leaves and lovely as flowers fallen beneath the trees, gathered up from below with the fingers, one could adorn your locks as if with blossoms.
t.8.73: O fair-faced one, this moon is being joined with the conjunction-star, whose disc is quivering, just as a bridegroom is joined with a newly consecrated maiden who has begun to tremble out of fear.
t.8.74: O you whose eyes are fixed upon the orb of the moon, the moonlight seems to spring up upon the curves of your cheeks, pale as reed stalks split open by ripeness and clear with the reflections that gleam across them.
t.8.75: Look, the presiding goddess of the Gandhamādana forest has come to you, steadfast in propriety, herself bearing the honey-wine of the wish-granting tree poured into a vessel of red sunstone.
t.8.76: Your face is by its very nature fragrant as fresh kesara blossoms, its eyes red as though with intoxication; once it has found its dwelling here, O playful one, what further charm can wine bestow?
t.8.77: "Or rather, your circle of friends is one whose devotion deserves honor; so let this drink, which kindles Love, be enjoyed." Having spoken thus graciously, Śaṅkara made Ambikā drink the wine.
t.8.78: Pārvatī, through partaking of it, underwent a transformation that charmed even the virtuous, wrought by union with an inscrutable decree, just as the common mango comes to be the fragrant sahakāra.
t.8.79: At that moment the fair-faced one came under the sway of two, of the Trident-bearer and of intoxication, both of whom had cast off shame, both of whom were about to lead her to the bed, and in both of whom passion was kindled.
t.8.80: With its eyes rolling, its words faltering, beaded with drops of sweat and smiling for no reason, Umā's face was long drunk in by the Lord, not yet with his mouth, but with his eye.
t.8.81: Carrying her, whose golden girdle hung loose and who was heavy to bear for the weight of her hips, the Lord, whose divine powers had been gathered through meditation, entered in private the chamber of jeweled stone.
t.8.82: There, accompanied by his beloved, he lay upon a bed whose coverlet was white as a haṃsa and which was lovely to behold like a sandbank of the Jāhnavī, as the lord of Rohiṇī rests upon an autumn cloud.
t.8.83: His lovemaking with Pārvatī, in which her hair was tangled, the sandal paste was rubbed away, nail marks were given in turn, each vied with the other, and her girdle-string snapped, did not bring him satiety.
t.8.84: Only when the rows of stars had sunk low did he, merciless toward his dearest, his chest held fast in her embrace, at last feel the desire to close his eyes.
t.8.85: At dawn he, the wise one, so fitting for you, awoke together with the pools of golden lotuses, while Kinnaras who had taken up the Kaiśika mode with its melodic modulations sang his auspicious songs.
t.8.87: At that moment Hara, his eyes captivated by the rows of nail-marks at the tops of her thighs, stopped his dearest beloved as she was fastening her loosened garment.
t.8.86: That couple, their embrace loosened for a moment, were attended by the breezes from the forest borders of Gandhamādana, which had set the waves of Lake Mānasa trembling and betrayed the blooming of the lotuses.
t.8.88: Gazing at his beloved's face, its eyes reddened from the sleepless night, its lower lip bruised by deep tooth-marks, its curls tousled and its tilaka smudged, he, full of passion, took his delight.
t.8.89: Even when the night had ended in clear daylight, he did not leave the bed, its coverlet rumpled and uneven with creases, a girdle with broken string lying bunched in its middle, and the whole marked with the red lac of her feet.
t.8.90: Wishing to savor day and night the nectar of his beloved's face, which made his joy ever grow, he became invisible to those who sought an audience with him, for Vijayā announced to them that he could not be seen.
t.8.91: For Śambhu, absorbed in love there, with day and night alike, more than a hundred seasons passed as though they were a single night; yet his thirst for the joys of lovemaking was never cut off, just as the fire that dwells within the ocean never ceases to thirst for its waters.
